meta.blurb: Epictetus was born a slave, tradition says, yet he taught that no one can take your inner freedom. His Enchiridion is a short handbook on what you control, what you do not, and how to stay calm either way.
meta.bible: The Enchiridion: a short handbook of 53 brief chapters of practical advice, compiled by Arrian from the teaching of Epictetus; the Greek title means something held in the hand, a handbook. Epictetus: a Greek Stoic philosopher born about AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey; tradition says he was born into slavery in Rome and was lame; he was freed, taught in Rome and later in Nicopolis in Greece, wrote nothing himself, and died about AD 135. Arrian: his student, who recorded his talks and gathered the Enchiridion. Stoicism: the school of philosophy that teaches that peace and goodness come from governing our own judgements and accepting what we cannot change. Socrates: the philosopher of Athens who died in 399 BC and whom Epictetus held up as a model. Chrysippus: a famous Stoic writer of the third century BC. Cleanthes: an earlier Stoic teacher whose prayer is quoted at the end. Euripides: the Greek poet quoted at the end. Anytus and Meletus: the men who accused Socrates. Zeus, the gods and Destiny: how Epictetus and the Stoics of his time spoke of the order of the world. Rome, Nicopolis, Greece: the places of his life. The Olympic Games: the athletic contest he uses as an image. Key idea: some things are up to us (our opinions, choices, wishes and actions) and some are not (our bodies, property, reputation and offices). Voice and tone: direct, practical, quietly humorous and firm; each beat names the chapter of the Enchiridion it comes from; everything is attributed to Epictetus; nothing is invented; respectful of every faith.

beats.scene: A lame old teacher speaks to students in a plain room in Greece
beats.summary: Introduces Epictetus, born a slave about AD 50, and his student Arrian, who gathered his teaching into the Enchiridion, a handbook.

beats.scene: A man holds a lamp while storm clouds gather over his house
beats.summary: Chapter 1: some things are up to us, such as opinions and actions, and some are not, such as bodies, money and fame.

beats.scene: A man struggles under a heavy sack of coins while another walks free
beats.summary: Chapter 1: what is up to us is free; what is not is weak, and mistaking one for the other brings trouble.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a clear road while a rocky mountain rises beyond
beats.summary: Chapter 2: aim your desire at what is up to you, and let go of dread of illness, death and poverty.

beats.scene: A woman pours water from a clay jug, then kisses her small child
beats.summary: Chapter 3: remember what each thing really is, from a jug to a loved one.

beats.scene: People splash, push and shout in a crowded public bath
beats.summary: Chapter 4: before you begin anything, think what it will really involve, like a trip to the public baths.

beats.scene: A man stares at a dark door, imagining a monster behind it
beats.summary: Chapter 5: people are upset not by things but by their opinions of them; death is not terrible in itself.

beats.scene: A man proudly leads a fine white horse down a village street
beats.summary: Chapter 6: do not be proud of what is not yours; only the right use of your own choices deserves pride.

beats.scene: A passenger picks up shells on the shore while the ship waits
beats.summary: Chapter 7: life is like a voyage; enjoy the stops, but be ready to leave when the captain calls.

beats.scene: A traveller smiles as rain falls on a muddy road
beats.summary: Chapter 8: do not ask that events happen as you wish; wish for them to happen as they do.

beats.scene: A lame traveller walks slowly with a stick and a calm face
beats.summary: Chapter 9: illness hinders the body, and lameness the leg, but neither hinders the will unless the will allows it.

beats.scene: A man stands calm and strong as wind and rain blow past him
beats.summary: Chapter 10: in every trouble ask what power you have within you to meet it.

beats.scene: A traveller leaves an inn at dawn and hands back the key
beats.summary: Chapter 11: never say you have lost something; say you have given it back, for everything is lent to us.

beats.scene: A boy spills a jar of oil while a man stays calm
beats.summary: Chapter 12: begin with small losses, and say that peace of mind is the price paid for them.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes stays quiet while others laugh at his clumsy answer
beats.summary: Chapter 13: be content to be thought foolish about outside things and do not try to seem wise.

beats.scene: A table of dishes passes slowly from hand to hand at a banquet
beats.summary: Chapter 15: treat life like a banquet; take politely what is passed to you and wait for what has not yet come.

beats.scene: A man sits beside a weeping friend and rests a hand on his shoulder
beats.summary: Chapter 16: comfort a grieving friend with kind words, but do not be swept away by his grief yourself.

beats.scene: An actor in a rough beggar's costume stands on a bare stage
beats.summary: Chapter 17: you are an actor in a play whose author chooses your part; your task is to play it well.

beats.scene: A black raven croaks from a bare branch above a quiet road
beats.summary: Chapter 18: do not be carried away by an omen such as a raven's croak; any sign can turn out well.

beats.scene: A calm athlete watches others compete in a distant arena
beats.summary: Chapter 19: you can be unbeatable if you enter only contests that you can win by your own effort.

beats.scene: A man laughs calmly as a neighbour shouts at him across a fence
beats.summary: Chapter 20: it is not the person who insults you who harms you but your own opinion that you are insulted.

beats.scene: A traveller with a small bag looks toward a far horizon at sunset
beats.summary: Chapter 21: keep death and exile before your eyes each day, so that nothing will seem mean and no wish will be too strong.

beats.scene: Friends laugh at a man holding a book while he stays calm
beats.summary: Chapter 22: if you turn to philosophy, be ready to be laughed at, and hold on to what you think is best.

beats.scene: Two men at a market stall: one pays coins, the other walks away empty-handed
beats.summary: Chapter 25: if another is honoured above you, ask what price you paid for it; a lettuce costs a small coin.

beats.scene: A servant drops a cup that shatters while a calm man looks on
beats.summary: Chapter 26: when another person's cup breaks we say it happens; we should react the same way when our own breaks.

beats.scene: A man hands the keys of his house to a rude stranger
beats.summary: Chapter 28: we would be angry if someone handed our body to a stranger, yet we hand our minds to anyone who insults us.

beats.scene: An athlete trains in the sun, sweating and covered in dust
beats.summary: Chapter 29: before you start anything, think what comes before and after, as in training for the Olympic Games.

beats.scene: A grown son helps his elderly father across a busy street
beats.summary: Chapter 30: duties are measured by relationships; do your part toward a father or brother even when he is hard to live with.

beats.scene: A man bows his head quietly before a simple stone altar
beats.summary: Chapter 31: the chief part of piety toward the gods is to hold right opinions about them and to accept what happens.

beats.scene: A quiet man listens at a table while others talk loudly
beats.summary: Chapter 33: be silent for the most part, speak only when needed, and never use words to gossip about others.

beats.scene: A man smiles gently while a gossiping neighbour points at him
beats.summary: Chapter 33: if you hear that someone has criticised you, answer that he does not know your other faults.

beats.scene: A man looks at a tempting cake on a table, then walks away smiling
beats.summary: Chapter 34: when a pleasure tempts you, let it wait, and picture how you will feel afterward.

beats.scene: A man works openly in a busy square while people stare
beats.summary: Chapter 35: when you do what you know is right, do not hide, even if people judge it badly.

beats.scene: A man walks carefully along a rocky path, watching his feet
beats.summary: Chapter 38: as you watch your steps to avoid a nail, take care not to harm the part of you that judges and chooses.

beats.scene: A shoemaker measures a foot beside a pile of fancy golden shoes
beats.summary: Chapter 39: the body is the measure of what we need to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe.

beats.scene: A man hurries through a quick meal, then sits down to read
beats.summary: Chapter 41: it is a sign of a dull mind to spend too long on the body; give it little time and the mind much.

beats.scene: Two men argue in a market while a third watches calmly
beats.summary: Chapter 42: when someone wrongs you, remember he does it because he thinks it right, and be gentle.

beats.scene: A man grips a large clay jar by its handle
beats.summary: Chapter 43: everything has two handles, one that can be carried and one that cannot; a brother is best held by the right one.

beats.scene: A rich man and a skilled speaker stand side by side, both looking proud
beats.summary: Chapter 44: I am richer than you does not mean I am better; it only means my property is greater.

beats.scene: A man gulps wine at a table while a friend watches without frowning
beats.summary: Chapter 45: do not say a man acts badly until you know why; say only what you actually saw.

beats.scene: A shepherd watches his sheep graze quietly in a green field
beats.summary: Chapter 46: do not show off your principles; sheep digest their grass and give wool and milk.

beats.scene: A man sips water quietly from a plain cup and says nothing
beats.summary: Chapter 47: when you have trained yourself to live simply, do not boast of it.

beats.scene: Two travellers on a road: one points at the weather, the other looks within
beats.summary: Chapter 48: the ordinary person expects help or harm from outside; the person making progress expects it only from himself.

beats.scene: A man receives praise with a private smile and walks on carefully
beats.summary: Chapter 48: the person making progress laughs quietly at praise, does not defend himself against blame, and guards what is healing.

beats.scene: A student proudly points at a thick scroll while a teacher shakes his head
beats.summary: Chapter 49: do not be proud of explaining the hard books of Chrysippus; what matters is to follow nature in deeds.

beats.scene: A man walks on steadily while others whisper behind his back
beats.summary: Chapter 50: keep the rules you have chosen as if they were laws, and do not mind what people say of you.

beats.scene: A grown man stands at a starting line as a crowd waits
beats.summary: Chapter 51: how long will you wait to demand the best of yourself?

beats.scene: A crowd gathers at the Olympic stadium as one man steps forward
beats.summary: Chapter 51: now is the contest; one day and one action can lose or save your progress, as Socrates showed.

beats.scene: A scholar reads a long argument about honesty to a patient friend
beats.summary: Chapter 52: the first part of philosophy is practising its lessons, then proving them, then testing the proofs; we reverse the order.

beats.scene: A man walks along a long road into the evening light, calm and unhurried
beats.summary: Chapter 53: three short sayings to keep ready: follow Destiny willingly, yield nobly to necessity, and remember that Socrates could not be truly harmed.

B1B2: Epictetus was born a slave about the year 50 AD and later became one of the most respected teachers of Stoic philosophy. His student Arrian wrote down his lessons and collected the best of them in a short handbook called the Enchiridion.
The Enchiridion begins by dividing the world into two parts. Some things, such as our opinions and actions, are up to us, but our bodies, money and fame are not.

Epictetus says that what is in our control is free, but what is outside it is weak and can be taken away. If we treat the second kind as if it belonged to us, he warns, we will be blocked, upset and angry.

In the second chapter, Epictetus says we should aim our wishes only at things that depend on us. If we dread illness, death or poverty, we will often be unhappy, because we cannot always keep them away.
Epictetus says that we should remember what each thing really is. If you love a clay cup, remind yourself that it is only a cup, and you will not be upset if it breaks.
Before doing anything, Epictetus says, we should stop and think about what it really involves. If you are going to the public baths, remember that people splash, push, shout and sometimes steal.
Epictetus says that people are disturbed not by things, but by their opinions about things. Death, for example, is not terrible in itself; what frightens us is our belief that it is terrible.
A man who is proud of his fine horse, Epictetus says, is proud of the horse's excellence and not his own. We should take pride only in what is truly ours, such as the way we think and choose.
In the seventh chapter, Epictetus compares life to a long sea voyage with many stops. You may enjoy the shore and pick up a shell, but you must be ready to leave the moment the captain calls.
Epictetus tells us not to ask that events happen as we wish, but to wish for events to happen as they do. If we learn to do this, he promises, we will be at peace.

Epictetus says that illness is an obstacle to the body, but not to the will, unless the will chooses to be stopped. The same is true of a lame leg, he says, for lameness slows us down but cannot stop our will.
Whatever happens to you, says Epictetus, ask what power you have within yourself to deal with it. Temptation calls for self-control, hard work for endurance, and an insult for patience.
Epictetus says that we should never say, “I have lost it,” but instead, “I have given it back.” Everything we have is only lent to us, so we should treat it as a traveller treats a room at an inn.
If you want to make progress, Epictetus says, start with small things. When oil is spilled or wine is stolen, tell yourself that this is the price of peace of mind.

If you want to make progress, says Epictetus, be willing to be thought foolish about things outside your control. Do not try to seem clever, and be happy to look ordinary while you work on your character.
Epictetus says that we should behave in life as we do at a banquet. Take politely what is passed to you, let go of what has passed, and wait for what has not yet come.

When you see someone crying over a loss, remember that his pain comes less from the loss than from his opinion of it. Do not hesitate to comfort him with words, and even to sigh with him, but take care not to cry inside.
Remember, says Epictetus, that you are an actor in a play, and the playwright chooses the part. Whether you play a beggar, a ruler or a private citizen, your job is to play the part well.
When a raven croaks, says Epictetus, do not let the sign carry you away. Tell yourself that it means nothing for you, since any sign can turn out well for the person who chooses to use it well.
Epictetus says that you can be unbeatable if you enter only contests where victory depends on you. Do not envy a person who is honoured or praised, because appearances can fool you.

Epictetus says that the person who insults you does not harm you; your own opinion that you are being insulted does. When someone makes you angry, remember that it is your own judgement that makes you angry.
Epictetus suggests that we keep death, exile and other terrible things in front of our eyes every day. If we do, he says, we will never think anything mean or want anything too much.
Epictetus warns that if you want to study philosophy, you must be ready to be laughed at. Do not look proud when they tease you, but hold on to what you think is best.
If someone gets more honour than you, Epictetus asks what you did to pay for it. A lettuce costs a small coin, he says, so the one who pays gets the lettuce and the one who does not pay goes without.
When someone else's cup is broken, says Epictetus, we say calmly that these things happen. When our own cup breaks, we should be just as calm, and we should treat greater losses in the same way.
Epictetus says that we would be angry if someone handed our body to any stranger. Yet we hand our minds to anyone who insults us and let them upset and confuse us.

In the twenty-ninth chapter, Epictetus says that we should consider what comes before and after any action. To win at the Olympic Games, you must follow a strict diet, train hard, and accept that you may be beaten.
Epictetus says that our duties are measured by our relationships. If your father is hard to live with, remember that you were given a father, not a perfect one, and do your part.
Epictetus says that the main part of respect for the gods is to hold right opinions about them. We should believe that they exist and that they govern the world well and fairly.

In the thirty-third chapter, Epictetus gives a long list of advice on how to behave in daily life. Be silent for the most part, he says, and speak only when you must, and never just to gossip about others.

If someone tells you that another person has spoken badly of you, Epictetus says, do not defend yourself. Just answer that he must not know your other faults, or he would not have mentioned only these.
When you imagine a pleasure, says Epictetus, do not let it carry you away. Let it wait, take some time, and think about how you will feel afterward, when you may regret it.

When you do something that you know is right, never hide from being seen, even if people will judge it badly. If it is wrong, do not do it, but if it is right, why fear those who criticise you wrongly?
As we watch our steps to avoid a nail, says Epictetus, we should take care not to harm our own mind. If we guard it in every action, we will act more safely.
Epictetus says that the body is the measure of what we own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. Stay within that measure and you will be content, but go beyond it and you may fall over a cliff.
Epictetus says it is a sign of a dull mind to spend too long on exercise, eating and drinking. These things should be done quickly, he says, and our real attention should go to the mind.
When someone harms you or speaks badly of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does it because he thinks it is right. If he is mistaken, he is the one who is harmed, because he is deceived.

Epictetus says that everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, remember that he grew up with you, and the weight will be easier to carry.

Epictetus says that it makes no sense to argue, “I am richer than you, so I am better.” It makes more sense to say, “I am richer than you, so my property is greater,” because you are not your property.
If a man bathes quickly, says Epictetus, do not say that he bathes badly, only that he bathes quickly. Until you know his reasons, how can you say that he is acting badly?

Epictetus says that you should never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk much about principles among those who do not study them. At a banquet, he says, do not explain how to eat, but simply eat as one should.
When you have trained your body to live simply, says Epictetus, do not boast about it. If you drink only water, do not say at every chance that you drink water.

In the forty-eighth chapter, Epictetus compares two ways of looking at life. The ordinary person expects help or harm from outside things, but the person who is growing wise expects them only from himself.

A person who is making progress quietly laughs at those who praise him, says Epictetus, and does not defend himself against blame. He moves like a person recovering from illness, careful not to disturb what is only beginning to heal.
Some people are proud of explaining the hard books of Chrysippus, says Epictetus, but such pride proves little. What matters is to follow nature, and to show by our deeds that we have understood.
Keep the rules that you have chosen, says Epictetus, as if they were laws that you must not break. Do not worry about what people say of you, because that is not up to you.

How long will you wait, asks Epictetus in the fifty-first chapter, before you demand the best of yourself? You are no longer a child, and if you keep putting things off, you may never notice that you are not improving.
Epictetus says that when something hard or pleasant is put in front of you, you should remember that now is the contest. Your progress can be lost or saved by one day and one action.

Epictetus says that the first and most necessary part of philosophy is putting its teachings into practice, for example, not lying. The second part is proving why we must not lie, and the third is the logic that tests the proofs.

The last chapter of the Enchiridion gathers three short sayings to keep in mind on every occasion. One promises to follow wherever destiny leads, and another calls wise the person who bows nobly to necessity.
C1C2: Epictetus was born into slavery in the Roman Empire about the year 50 AD, and tradition says that he was lame, perhaps from the cruelty of a master. After he was freed, he became one of the most respected teachers of Stoic philosophy, first in Rome and later in Nicopolis in Greece. He wrote nothing himself, but his student Arrian recorded his talks and gathered the most useful of them into a pocket-sized handbook, the Enchiridion, whose name means something held in the hand.

Epictetus opens his handbook with a single clean division of the world into what depends on us and what does not. Our opinions, our impulses, our desires and our aversions are our own doing, he says, whereas our bodies, our property, our reputations and our public offices are not. Almost everything else in the book, as we shall see, grows out of this one distinction, and every chapter returns to it.

What is within our power is free by nature, Epictetus explains, and no one can stop it or hold it back, while what is not within our power is weak, slavish and always open to being taken by others. If we mistake the second kind for our own, we will find ourselves hindered, grieved and in turmoil, and we will blame gods and men alike. But if we claim as ours only what truly is ours, no one will ever be able to force us or hinder us, and we will have no enemy and suffer no harm.

The second chapter applies this idea to desire and dread, the two forces that most often disturb the mind. A person who desires what he cannot control will be disappointed, Epictetus says, and one who dreads what he cannot avoid will be wretched. Aim your wishes at the things that are truly yours, and for the present let your dislike of illness, death and poverty fall quiet.

In the third chapter Epictetus teaches us to ask what a thing truly is, starting with the smallest and working toward the greatest. If you are fond of a clay jug, he says, remind yourself that it is a clay jug, and then you will not be disturbed when it breaks. In the same spirit, when you kiss your child or your wife, tell yourself that you are kissing a human being, so that if death comes you will not be thrown into confusion.

The fourth chapter offers a lesson in preparing the mind for the ordinary troubles of the day. Whenever you are about to begin something, Epictetus says, remind yourself what that activity is like; if you are going to the public baths, picture the people splashing, pushing, shouting and even stealing. Then you may say, with a steady heart, that you intend to bathe and to keep your own will in harmony with nature, so that whatever happens, you are not surprised.

One of the best-known passages of the Enchiridion, in the fifth chapter, claims that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by the opinions they hold about those things. Death, for example, is nothing terrible, or Socrates would have thought it so, and the terror lies only in our judgment that death is terrible. So when we are thwarted, upset or distressed, he says, we should never blame others but ourselves, which is to say our own opinions.

Epictetus has a gentle way of puncturing vanity: if a horse were to boast that it is beautiful, he says, we could bear it, but if you boast that you own one, you are proud of the horse's good. The sixth chapter asks what is really ours, and it answers that only the right use of our own impressions and choices deserves such pride. Everything else, whether a house, a title or a fine horse, is borrowed, and the borrowed gives no true grounds for boasting.

In the seventh chapter life becomes a long voyage by sea, and we are its passengers rather than its owners. When the ship stops at a harbour, Epictetus says, you may walk ashore to fetch water and pick up a shell, but your mind must remain on the ship, listening for the captain's call. In just the same way, we may enjoy a wife, a child or a house as small gifts along the road, so long as we are ready to leave them behind.

The eighth chapter contains one of the boldest and most misunderstood suggestions in the whole book. Do not seek for events to happen as you wish, Epictetus advises, but wish them to happen as they do happen, and your life will flow on smoothly. It does not mean that we must never try to improve the world, but that our inner peace should not wait upon the outcome.

The ninth chapter turns to illness and lameness, a subject on which Epictetus, who was lame himself, wrote with some authority. Sickness, he says, is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses to be hindered; lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to the will. Say this to yourself about everything that befalls you, he urges, and you will find that whatever happens may hinder something else but never yourself.

The tenth chapter hands us a practical question to ask whenever something befalls us: what power do I have within me to meet this? When you see an attractive person, Epictetus says, you will find that you have self-control, when hard work faces you, endurance, and when someone abuses you, patience. If you form this habit, you will not be carried away by your impressions, but will treat each hardship as an invitation to use a strength that you already own.

The eleventh chapter offers a gentle and difficult answer to the experience of loss. Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” Epictetus advises, but say, “I have given it back,” whether it is a child who has died, a farm that has been taken or a fortune that has slipped away. Whatever we have, we hold only while the giver allows, and so we should care for it as travellers care for a room in an inn.

In the twelfth chapter Epictetus recommends that anyone who wishes to make progress should begin with small losses and work upward. When a little oil is spilled or a little wine is stolen, say to yourself that this is the price paid for calm and for freedom from disturbance, for nothing is got for nothing. And when you call a servant, remember that he may not come, or may not do as you ask, but he is not so important that your peace of mind should depend upon him.

The thirteenth chapter makes an unusual request of anyone who wants to improve, and it is not an easy one to grant. Be content, Epictetus says, to be thought foolish and ignorant about outside matters such as wealth and reputation, and do not wish to appear to know anything about them. If you are ever taken for someone important, he adds, be suspicious of yourself, because it is hard to keep your choices in harmony with nature while also securing a fine reputation.

Life, Epictetus says in the fifteenth chapter, should be treated like a banquet, with all the good manners that a banquet requires. When a dish is handed round and comes to you, take a modest portion; when it passes, do not call it back; and when it has not yet arrived, do not reach out for it, but wait until it comes. Do this with children, with a wife, with office and with wealth, he promises, and one day you will deserve to dine at the table of the gods.

Epictetus was not asking us to be cold, as the sixteenth chapter makes clear, and his advice for a grieving friend is a model of balance. When you see someone weeping for a lost child or lost property, he says, do not be swept away by the impression that something terrible has happened, but remember that it is the person's opinion that distresses him. Speak kindly to him, and even sigh with him if the moment calls for it, only take care that you do not also sigh in your own heart.

The seventeenth chapter gives us a famous image: you are an actor in a play, and the playwright decides what kind of play it will be. If he wants it short, it will be short, and if he wants it long, it will be long, and if he wishes you to play a beggar or a ruler, you must act that part with skill. Your task, Epictetus says, is only to play the given part well, for choosing the part belongs to someone else.

In the eighteenth chapter a raven croaks, and the ancient world would have taken the sound as a warning of disaster. Do not be carried away by the impression, Epictetus tells us, but say to yourself that none of this signifies anything for you, but only for your poor body, your small property, your name or your family. Everything, in his view, is a favourable sign for the person who chooses to see it so, because whatever happens, it is in that person's power to draw some benefit from it.

You can be unbeatable, Epictetus says in the nineteenth chapter, if you never enter a contest whose outcome does not depend on you. So do not be dazzled when you see someone honoured above others or holding great power, for the impression of happiness is often only an impression, and it may carry you into a servitude of your own making. Seek your victory where it can truly be won, in the quiet field of your own judgement.

The twentieth chapter tackles a problem we all know too well: how to bear an insult without losing our temper. It is not the man who abuses you or strikes you who injures you, Epictetus says, but your own opinion that these things are injurious, so when someone irritates you, it is your own judgement that has irritated you. Therefore, try not to be swept away by the first impression, for if you can gain a little time, you will find it much easier to master yourself.

In the twenty-first chapter Epictetus offers advice that may sound grim but is meant to be freeing. Keep death and exile and all the things that seem terrible daily before your eyes, he says, and above all keep death, and you will never entertain a mean thought or desire anything to excess. The aim is not to dwell in gloom but to see that these things are part of the human lot, so that they lose their power to surprise and to rule us.

If you want to study philosophy, Epictetus says in the twenty-second chapter, prepare to be laughed at, for many people will jeer that you have come back to them a philosopher and will ask where you found your sudden airs. Do not put on such airs, he advises, but hold fast to what seems best to you, as though you had been given a post to guard that you must not abandon. If you persist, those who first mocked you will in time admire you, but if you give way, you will be laughed at twice.

In the twenty-fifth chapter someone is preferred to you at a dinner or in a greeting or when advice is sought, and Epictetus asks whether you are upset. How can you expect the same rewards, he asks, when you have not paid the price that they cost? A lettuce costs a small coin, so the one who pays receives the lettuce, and the one who does not pay still has his coin and loses nothing.

The twenty-sixth chapter finds a lesson in a broken cup, and the lesson reaches much further than crockery. When a servant breaks another man's cup, Epictetus observes, we say at once that these things happen, and so when our own cup breaks we should be exactly as we were when the other broke. Carry the same attitude to greater things, he says, remembering how calmly we speak when the child or wife of another person dies, and how loudly we mourn when our own is lost.

Imagine that someone gave your body to any passing stranger, Epictetus says in the twenty-eighth chapter, and you would be furious. Yet you hand your own mind to whoever happens to insult you, letting it be disturbed and thrown into confusion by a few careless words, and you feel no shame at the exchange. The mind is the most precious thing we own, he reminds us, and it should be guarded at least as carefully as the body.

Before you begin any task, Epictetus advises in the twenty-ninth chapter, think carefully about what comes before it and what follows, or you will start with enthusiasm and quit in shame. If you want to win at the Olympic Games, consider what is demanded: a strict diet, training at fixed hours in heat and cold, and no wine or cold drinks at will. Count the cost first, he says, and if you still wish to compete, go, but otherwise you will be like children who play at wrestlers one day and gladiators the next and never finish anything.

Duties, according to the thirtieth chapter, are measured by relationships, and Epictetus gives the example of a father: you are to take care of him, to yield to him in everything, and to bear it patiently when he is harsh. But he is a bad father, you may object, and the answer is that nature gave you a father, not a good father. If a brother wrongs you, keep your own place toward him, and look not at what he does, but at what you must do to keep your own choices in accord with nature.

Speaking from within his own tradition, Epictetus says in the thirty-first chapter that the chief element of piety toward the gods is to hold right opinions about them, believing that they exist and govern the universe well and justly. We should therefore arrange ourselves to obey them, to yield to whatever happens, and to follow events willingly, as things brought about by the highest intelligence. In this way, he promises, we will never blame the gods or accuse them of neglecting us.

The thirty-third chapter is one of the longest, a list of advice on conduct that reads like a rule of life. Be silent for the most part, Epictetus says, or say only what is necessary and in few words; speak rarely, and not about gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink, which are the common topics of the day. Above all, do not talk about people by blaming, praising or comparing them, and if you can, lead the talk of your companions toward something worthy.

Epictetus has a witty answer for gossip, also in the thirty-third chapter, and it deserves to be remembered. If someone tells you that another person has spoken ill of you, do not defend yourself against the charge, but reply that he must be unaware of your other faults, or he would not have mentioned only these. The same chapter advises us to avoid long stories about our own deeds and dangers, which are never as interesting to others as they are to us.

The thirty-fourth chapter offers a simple method for dealing with temptation, and it is a method that anyone can try at once. When you receive the impression of some pleasure, do not be carried away, but let the matter wait, and then picture both moments: the time when you will enjoy it and the time afterwards when you will regret it. Set against these how glad you will be if you refrain, and if it still seems right to act, take care that its sweetness does not overcome you.

The thirty-fifth chapter is brief, but it asks for a good deal of courage from anyone who takes it seriously. Whenever you do something that you have judged to be right, Epictetus says, never try to avoid being seen doing it, even if most people think badly of it. If the action is wrong you should not do it, and if it is right, why fear those who rebuke you wrongly, for courage of this kind belongs not to the loud but to the steady?

In the thirty-eighth chapter, Epictetus compares the care we take of our feet with the care we ought to take of our minds. Just as, when we walk, we take care not to step on a nail or twist an ankle, so we should take care not to harm the ruling part of ourselves, the faculty that judges and chooses. If we guard it in every action, he says, we will set about everything more safely.

The thirty-ninth chapter has a plain and practical lesson about how much we need to own. The body is the measure of each person's property, Epictetus says, as the foot is the measure of the shoe, and if you stop at that limit, you will keep the right measure. If you go past it, however, you will be swept along as if over a cliff, for the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered, and once the measure is passed, there is no limit at all.

The forty-first chapter warns against a quiet kind of imbalance in the way we spend our days. It is a sign of a dull nature, Epictetus says, to spend a great deal of time on matters that concern the body, such as long exercise, long meals and long drinking. All these things should be done in passing, he insists, while the whole of our real attention is turned to the improvement of the mind.

The forty-second chapter urges us to look at wrongdoers with a more patient eye. Remember, Epictetus says, that when a person harms you or speaks ill of you, he does so because he thinks it right; he cannot follow what seems right to you, but only what seems right to him. If he is wrong, he is the one who is harmed, since he is the one who has been deceived, and this thought will teach you to be gentle with those who abuse you.

One of the most memorable images in the book comes in the forty-third chapter: everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, Epictetus says, do not take hold of the matter by the handle of the wrong, but by the other handle, that he is your brother and was brought up with you. In this way, you will pick up the burden by the handle that lets you bear it.

The forty-fourth chapter points out a flaw in the way we measure ourselves, and it is one that we still commit every day. It makes no sense to reason that I am richer than you, and therefore better than you, or that I am more eloquent than you, and therefore better, says Epictetus. The sound conclusions are instead that my property is greater than yours, or that my speech is finer than yours, but you are neither property nor speech, and a person's worth lies somewhere else.

The forty-fifth chapter teaches patience in judgement, and it begins with two small examples from everyday life. If someone bathes quickly, Epictetus says, do not say that he bathes badly, but that he bathes quickly; if someone drinks a great deal of wine, do not say that he drinks badly, but that he drinks a great deal. Until you know what he believes, how can you know that he is acting wrongly, and by waiting, you will avoid approving impressions that may prove false.

The forty-sixth chapter has no patience for show, and it is blunt about the danger of lecturing others. Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and do not talk much among ordinary people about your principles, but act on them: at a banquet, do not explain how one ought to eat, but eat as one ought. Sheep do not bring their shepherd the grass to prove how much they have eaten, he says, but digest it and give wool and milk, and so we should show not theories but the actions that grow from them.

In the forty-seventh chapter, Epictetus turns to modest living and the temptation to boast of it. When you have adapted your body to simple fare, he says, do not make a show of it, and if you drink only water, do not announce at every opportunity that you drink only water. If you ever wish to train yourself in hardship, do it for yourself and not for outsiders; when you are very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.

The forty-eighth chapter draws a portrait of two different characters, and the contrast between them is sharp. The ordinary person, Epictetus says, looks for benefit and harm from outside things, whereas the philosopher looks for both only from himself, and a sign of progress is that he blames, praises and complains of no one. He does not speak of himself as if he were somebody, and when he is hindered, he blames only himself.

When he is praised, the person who is making progress laughs quietly at the one who praises him, says Epictetus, and when he is blamed, he does not defend himself. He goes about like a convalescent, careful not to disturb any part that is beginning to heal until it has grown firm. His impulses are gentle, he does not mind seeming foolish or ignorant, and he watches himself as one would watch an enemy lying in ambush.

Chrysippus was a famous Stoic who wrote hundreds of books, and the forty-ninth chapter laughs gently at those who take pride in explaining them. If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, Epictetus says, such a man would have nothing to be proud of. What Epictetus himself wants is to understand nature and follow it, and he adds that if he merely admired the explanations, he would be a scholar of words and not a philosopher.

The fiftieth chapter is a call to steadiness, and its advice is simple to say and hard to do. Stand firmly by whatever rules you have laid down for yourself, Epictetus says, as though they were laws that it would be wrong to break, and pay no attention to what others say, for that is not in your power. Praise and blame are weather, in other words, and a person who sails by his own compass need not look up at every cloud.

The fifty-first chapter is a challenge, and it is addressed directly to every reader of the book. How long will you wait, Epictetus asks, before you demand the best of yourself and in nothing go against the verdict of reason? You have already received the principles you ought to accept, and you have accepted them, so what sort of teacher do you still wait for, and why are you leaving your improvement to him?

So decide now, Epictetus urges, to live as a mature person who is making progress, and let whatever seems best be a law that cannot be broken. If anything laborious or pleasant, glorious or inglorious is set before you, remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic Games, and they cannot be put off, for progress is lost or saved by one day. Socrates became what he was in just this way, attending to nothing but reason, and you ought to live as one who wishes to become him.

Philosophy, Epictetus explains in the fifty-second chapter, has three parts, and the order of importance is the one that matters. The first and most necessary is putting its teachings into practice, as in the rule that we must not lie, the second is proving why we must not lie, and the third is the logic that tests the proofs. We tend to reverse them, he complains, spending all our time on the third and ignoring the first, so that we go on lying even though we have a perfect argument ready to show why lying is wrong.

The Enchiridion closes with three short quotations that, Epictetus says, we should keep ready on every occasion. The first, a prayer by the Stoic Cleanthes, asks Zeus and Destiny to lead us wherever they please and promises to follow without hesitation, while the second, from the poet Euripides, calls wise anyone who has nobly yielded to necessity. The third is the calm word of Socrates, that his accusers could kill him but never truly harm him, and together they sum up the book: peace comes from meeting the world with a steady heart.
